headline: High-risk shared-write and shared-context pair: default configs can leak data and cascade errors across OpenHands and semantica.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can use MCP and reads/writes runtime files; semantica also uses MCP and ingests many file and message surfaces. If semantica outputs are placed into the shared mounted volume or MCP channel, OpenHands may treat attacker-controlled content as instructions. The pathway is plausible from both profiles, though not directly documented.
conditions: IF semantica writes untrusted content into a shared file or MCP resource consumed by OpenHands
IF OpenHands parses semantica-produced text as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Separate the agents onto distinct workspaces
Disable MCP sharing between the pair
Add a strict content boundary for semantica outputs
Require manual review before OpenHands acts on semantica text

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands touches files mounted into its runtime and handles model-provider API keys; semantica touches enterprise data, contracts, audit trails, and secrets. Because both can read/write files and use MCP, a shared workspace or shared context layer can expose sensitive semantica data to OpenHands and onward to its model provider. The blast radius includes exfiltration and compliance breach.
conditions: IF both agents access the same mounted volume or shared MCP resources
IF semantica stores enterprise data or secrets in files OpenHands can read
IF OpenHands sends those contents to its model provider
mitigations: Use separate volumes for each agent
Remove secrets from shared files before either agent runs
Restrict OpenHands to non-sensitive directories
Turn off MCP resource sharing
requires-engineering: add per-agent provenance and redaction gates

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files, modify git state, install packages, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. OpenHands runs in a Docker runtime with broad egress, while semantica operates over a shared intelligence layer and multiple mutable enterprise sources. Concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace can corrupt state or overwrite each other's changes without locking.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository or directory
IF no external lock or lease is enforced
IF either agent performs concurrent package installs or file writes
mitigations: Assign separate repos or branches
Add a file-locking wrapper around shared paths
Serialize package installation steps
Pause one agent while the other mutates git state
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency checks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Semantica's shared context graph and provenance features can ingest OpenHands outputs, while OpenHands can generate code, facts, or edits from browser and shell actions. If semantica treats those outputs as authoritative, errors can propagate into downstream records, decisions, or commits. The pair lacks a documented verification barrier in the profiles, so uncertainty pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF semantica ingests OpenHands-generated text into its shared context graph
IF downstream consumers trust that graph without independent verification
IF OpenHands outputs contain an error or hallucination
mitigations: Require human review before ingestion
Tag OpenHands outputs as untrusted provenance
Add validation rules before graph writes
Compare outputs against source files or APIs
requires-engineering: enforce verification checkpoints

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands is documented as handling model-provider API keys and running with broad egress, while semantica is documented to touch enterprise data, contracts, audit trails, and secrets. If regulated or sensitive data flows from semantica into OpenHands, the pair can create residency, retention, or third-party transfer issues. The profiles do not show a shared compliance boundary, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF semantica processes regulated enterprise data or secrets
IF OpenHands receives that data through files, MCP, or prompts
IF OpenHands forwards content to a third-party model provider
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of OpenHands inputs
Use a DPA-approved backend for any shared data
Redact secrets before transfer
Set retention limits on shared artifacts
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
